entities.name: Konstantinos Aspietes
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Konstantinos Aspietes emerged as a formidable Byzantine general during a tumultuous period marked by internal strife and external pressures in the late 12th and early 13th centuries. His career, primarily under Emperor Alexios III Angelos (reigned 1195–1203), was characterized by tenacious military campaigns against the resurgent Second Bulgarian Empire and involvement in the complex political landscape of the declining Komnenian-Angeloi dynasty. Aspietes's strategic acumen and battlefield leadership made him a crucial figure in defending the empire's northern frontiers, even as the heart of Byzantium was increasingly vulnerable to both internal dissent and foreign aggression.

Aspietes achieved significant successes in his campaigns against the Bulgarians, particularly during the early years of Alexios III's reign. He commanded forces in Thrace and Macedonia, regions frequently contested by Bulgarian incursions, and his efforts helped to temporarily stabilize these volatile borders. However, his rise also coincided with the Byzantine court's endemic paranoia; Emperor Alexios III, fearing Aspietes's growing influence and popularity, ordered his blinding—a common Byzantine punishment for perceived threats to imperial power—around 1201. Despite this brutal incapacitation, Aspietes remained a symbol of Byzantine military resilience, potentially offering counsel or lending his name to resistance efforts even after losing his sight.
